title: India Plans $1.2 Billion Incentive to Build Construction Equipment and Cut China Dependence
excerpt: The seven-year scheme targets tunnel boring machines, elevators, and fire-fighting equipment — sectors where India remains heavily reliant on Chinese imports for metro rail and highway construction.
body:
• India is set to approve a $1.2 billion incentive scheme for domestic manufacturing of high-value construction and infrastructure equipment, including tunnel boring machines, elevators, and fire-fighting equipment, according to two government sources cited by Reuters.
  • The scheme aims to attract $1.8 billion in fresh investment over seven years and will include local value-addition targets for machines currently imported in full.
  • India remains heavily dependent on Chinese-supplied tunnel boring machines used in metro rail and highway construction — a vulnerability exposed when Chinese export controls delayed German-made machines produced in Chinese facilities.
  • Potential beneficiaries include state-run BEML, Larsen and Toubro, and Johnson Lifts, with final Cabinet approval expected soon.

The Incentive Plan

India is preparing to approve a $1.2 billion incentive scheme to boost domestic manufacturing of technologically sophisticated construction and infrastructure equipment, two government sources told Reuters. The scheme, expected to be finalized soon, aims to draw $1.8 billion in fresh investment over seven years.

The incentives will target manufacturers of equipment including tunnel boring machines, fire-fighting equipment, and elevators used in high-rise buildings. The plan was first announced in the 2026-27 Union Budget by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, who said the equipment covered could range from "lifts in a multi-story apartment, fire-fighting equipment, large and small, to tunnel-boring equipment for building metros and high-altitude roads."

The scheme has been designed after assessing the incentives required to make local production viable against India's existing import dependence, the sources said. It will also include targets for local value addition for machines that are presently fully imported.

The China Vulnerability

India's construction and infrastructure equipment market is valued at approximately 1 trillion rupees ($10.5 billion) and is set to expand rapidly as the country accelerates spending on roads, metros, airports, and other infrastructure. Capital expenditure across mining and construction equipment-linked sectors is projected to rise from about 5.5 lakh crore rupees in 2025 to 9-10 lakh crore rupees by 2030.

But a significant share of the high-value equipment — particularly tunnel boring machines — is imported, with China among the key suppliers. The vulnerability became tangible when Chinese export controls delayed delivery of tunnel boring machines manufactured by German company Herrenknecht at facilities in China, stalling Indian projects worth billions of dollars.

The TBM delays drew attention because they affected high-profile infrastructure projects. But the deeper significance was what they revealed about India's dependence on overseas manufacturing for specialized equipment — and how geopolitical tensions, export restrictions, or supply chain disruptions can directly affect project timelines. As India expands metro networks, develops high-speed rail, and undertakes increasingly complex infrastructure projects, demand for technologically advanced equipment will rise sharply.

Who Benefits

The incentive plan could benefit state-run BEML, which has plans to domestically manufacture tunnel boring machines. Other potential beneficiaries include Larsen and Toubro, one of India's largest engineering and construction conglomerates, and Johnson Lifts, a major elevator manufacturer.

India has built considerable capabilities in conventional construction machinery — global firms such as Caterpillar, Komatsu, and JCB all have manufacturing operations in the country, and domestic players have expanded significantly. Yet many advanced systems and high-value components continue to be sourced from abroad.

"Lifts in a multi-story apartment, fire-fighting equipment, large and small, to tunnel-boring equipment for building metros and high-altitude roads."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister, describing equipment covered by the new scheme

Previous Incentive Schemes: Mixed Track Record

The new scheme arrives against the backdrop of India's broader manufacturing push, which has delivered mixed results. The government's $23 billion Production-Linked Incentive scheme, launched across 14 sectors to woo firms away from China, has been allowed to lapse. While mobile phones and consumer electronics were bright spots, many participating firms failed to meet production targets, and India had issued just $1.73 billion in incentives — under 8% of allocated funds — by October 2024, according to a commerce ministry analysis seen by Reuters.

Since the PLI scheme's introduction, manufacturing's share of India's economy has actually decreased from 15.4% to 14.3%. The new construction equipment scheme appears to be more narrowly targeted, focusing on specific product categories where the import dependence is acute and where domestic production is technically feasible with the right incentives.

"The scheme was announced in the 2026-27 Union Budget to strengthen domestic production of high-value, technologically advanced construction and infrastructure equipment."

— News Insight, citing Union Budget announcement

Broader Manufacturing Push

The construction equipment incentive is part of a wider effort by the Modi government to reduce reliance on critical imports. India recently identified $51 billion in imports across multiple sectors that could be manufactured domestically, and the government is encouraging joint ventures with firms from Taiwan, South Korea, Germany, and Italy to narrow the capability gap.

India's imports from China stood at nearly $132 billion in fiscal year 2025-26 — the highest from any single country — including inputs and machinery critical to the functioning of Indian factories. For Indian companies and NRI investors watching India's infrastructure buildout, the new scheme signals both an opportunity and an acknowledgment that previous approaches have fallen short of ambitions.
